message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary at /workspace/dataset/test15_executable.
DO NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk anyway).
DO NOT use `strings`, `objdump`, `nm`, `gdb`, or any binary/symbol inspection. Behavioral probing via command-line arguments ONLY.

The binary's driver program is exactly this:

  inflection::Inflector::initialize();
  std::vector<std::string> results;
  for (int i = 1; i < argc && i <= 5; i++) {
      std::string word = argv[i];
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::pluralize(word));
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::camelize(word));
      if (i % 2 == 0) results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::underscore(word));
  }
  for (const auto& r : results) std::cout << r << std::endl;
  if (argc > 1) {
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isPlural(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isSingular(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::demodulize("Module::" + std::string(argv[1])) << std::endl;
  }

So to observe a function on an arbitrary word W:
  - pluralize(W)  -> line 1 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - camelize(W)   -> line 2 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - underscore(W) -> `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable dummy "W"` prints: pluralize(dummy), camelize(dummy), pluralize(W), camelize(W), underscore(W), then isPlural/isSingular/demodulize of "dummy". So underscore(W) is line 5.
  - isPlural(W)   -> line 3 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"` (prints as 0/1 since it's a bool via operator<<)
  - isSingular(W) -> line 4 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - demodulize("Module::" + W) -> line 5 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`

Run MANY probes (hundreds). Use bash loops. Quote arguments properly. Capture stderr too (2>&1 separately from stdout when it matters) and capture exit codes.
Be systematic: form a hypothesis, then design inputs that DISCRIMINATE between competing hypotheses, then confirm.
Report the exact rule as precise pseudocode operating on BYTES (the C++ code uses std::string = bytes; the "C" locale means std::toupper/tolower only affect ASCII a-z/A-Z). Explicitly test non-ASCII UTF-8 input to confirm byte-level behavior.


=== YOUR DIMENSION: demodulize ===

Derive the COMPLETE behavior of inflection::Inflector::demodulize.

Observe: line 5 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"` is demodulize("Module::" + W). Note the input ALWAYS has the literal 8-byte prefix "Module::".

Initial probing: W="cat" -> "at"; W="person" -> "erson"; W="a" -> ""; W="" -> the program CRASHES with std::out_of_range (substr __pos 9 > size 8). So there is an off-by-one: it skips 3 bytes past the found position of "::" instead of 2.

Competing hypotheses to DISCRIMINATE:
  (a) pos = rfind("::"); return s.substr(pos + 3)
  (b) pos = find("::");  return s.substr(pos + 3)
  (c) pos = rfind(':');  return s.substr(pos + 2)
  (d) pos = find(':');   return s.substr(pos + 3)
  (e) pos = rfind(':');  return s.substr(pos + 1) + something ... (consider others too)

Discriminating inputs (remember "Module::" is prepended):
  W = "A::B"   -> full input "Module::A::B" (len 12): (a)-> substr(12)="" ; (b)-> substr(9)="A::B" ; (c) rfind(':')=10 -> substr(12)="" ; (d)-> substr(9)="A::B"
  W = "a:b"    -> full input "Module::a:b" (len 11): (a) rfind("::")=6 -> substr(9)=":b" ; (c) rfind(':')=9 -> substr(11)=""
  W = "x::y::z", W = ":", W = "::", W = ":::", W = "a::", W = "::a", W = "a:", W = ":a"
Work out the predictions for each hypothesis yourself and run them ALL. Determine which single hypothesis explains every observation.

Also:
1. Characterize EXACTLY when it crashes (out_of_range) vs returns a value. Capture the exact stderr text and the exit code (use `; echo "exit=$?"`). Report the exact stderr bytes.
2. Test W values: "", "a", "ab", ":", "::", ":::", "::::", "a::", "::a", "a::b", "a::b::c", "x:y", "Module::x", "A::B::C::D", strings with trailing colons, whitespace.
3. Non-ASCII: W = "café", "日本語" — is the result a byte slice (possibly splitting a UTF-8 sequence)? Verify with `od -c`. This matters a lot: a Rust port must slice BYTES, not chars, and must not panic on invalid UTF-8 boundaries. Find an input where the C++ output is INVALID UTF-8 (e.g. W = "é" gives input "Module::é" where skipping 3 bytes from pos 6 lands mid-sequence — work it out and test).
4. Determine what happens with no "::" at all — you cannot test directly since "Module::" is always prepended, so instead REASON about it and state that the port only needs to be correct for inputs containing "::" (but suggest a safe fallback).

Report the single confirmed hypothesis with the evidence that rules out the others, plus a rich golden set including the crash case (exact stderr + exit code).

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). cd /workspace/dataset
# build word list in bash
alpha=(a b ':' x Y _ ' ' - '::' ':::' 'é' 'q')
words=("")
for i in $(seq 1 600); do
  L=$(( (RANDOM % 5) + 1 )); w=""
  for j in $(seq 1 $L); do w="$w${alpha[$((RANDOM % ${#alpha[@]}))]}"; done
  words+=("$w")
done
fail=0; n=0
for w in "${words[@]}"; do
  n=$((n+1))
  s="Module::$w"
  # last colon index (byte) via bash: strip longest suffix without ':'
  case "$s" in *:*) pre="${s%:*}"; pos=${#pre}; ;; *) pos=-1;; esac
  len=${#s}
  if [ $((pos+2)) -gt $len ]; then exp="__CRASH__"; else exp="${s:$((pos+2))}"; fi
  ./test15_executable "$w" >/tmp/o 2>/dev/null; ec=$?
  if [ "$exp" = "__CRASH__" ]; then
    [ $ec -eq 0 ] && { echo "MISS-no-crash w=[$w]"; fail=1; }
  else
    [ $ec -ne 0 ] && { echo "MISS-crash w=[$w]"; fail=1; continue; }
    got=$(sed -n '5p' /tmp/o)
    [ "$got" != "$exp" ] && { echo "MISS-out w=[$w] got=[$got] exp=[$exp]"; fail=1; }
  fi
done
echo "tested=$n fail=$fail"

Every one of ~660 probes (20 hand-picked discriminators + 601 randomized words over the alphabet {a,b,':','::',':::',x,Y,_,space,-,'é',q} + non-ASCII + long strings) matched this model exactly, with zero mismatches in both value and crash/no-crash.

RULED OUT (e)-style two-step forms such as s.substr(pos+1).substr(1): the exception message names a single substr with __pos measured against the FULL string length (W="" -> "__pos (which is 9) > this->size() (which is 8)"; a two-step form would report __pos 1 > size 0). So it is one substr call on the whole string.

CONFIRMED (c): pos = rfind(':') (single byte 0x3A), return substr(pos + 2). Verified independently by the crash arithmetic: for every crashing input the message is exactly '__pos (which is N+1) > this->size() (which is N)' with N = 8 + byte_len(W) — consistent with last colon at index N-1 and start = N+1.
The search target is a SINGLE ':' byte, not the digraph "::": W="a:bc" -> "c" (last colon at input index 9, single, preceded by 'a').
Skip is a uniform +2 regardless of what precedes the last colon: W="a:bc" -> "c" and W="a::bc" -> "c" (last colon at 9 vs 10, both +2).
Byte comparison is exact/unsigned: W="\xba\xbab" (0xBA = 0x3A|0x80) -> result bytes ba 62, i.e. the 0xBA bytes were NOT treated as colons (pos stayed at 7 from the "Module::" prefix).
Other punctuation is not a separator: W="a;b" -> ";b", W="a.b" -> ".b", W="a/b" -> "/b", W="a|b" -> "|b" (all just input[9..], pos=7).

No case folding, trimming, or any other transformation: W="FooBar" -> "ooBar", W="HTTPServer" -> "TTPServer", W="no_colons_here" -> "o_colons_here", W="a::b " -> " " (trailing space preserved), W="a\tb" -> "\tb".

CRASH CONDITION (exact): std::out_of_range is thrown iff the LAST BYTE of the input string is ':' (equivalently, for this driver, iff W is empty or W's last byte is ':'). All other inputs return normally, possibly the empty string. Verified over 601 random inputs: crash <=> input ends with ':' held in every case.

Result is a raw BYTE slice with no UTF-8 awareness. W="é" (c3 a9) -> input "Module::" + c3 a9 (len 10), pos=7, substr(9) = single byte a9 = a lone UTF-8 continuation byte => INVALID UTF-8 output. W="日本語" (e6 97 a5 e6 9c ac e8 aa 9e) -> substr(9) = 97 a5 e6 9c ac e8 aa 9e, starts with continuation byte 0x97 => INVALID UTF-8. W="🎉" (f0 9f 8e 89) -> 9f 8e 89 => INVALID UTF-8. W="ü" (c3 bc) -> bc. W="€" (e2 82 ac) -> 82 ac.
W="café" -> "afé" (61 66 c3 a9) which happens to stay valid UTF-8 — so validity is incidental, purely a function of where byte 9 lands.

Length arithmetic is in bytes, confirmed via crash message: W="é:" (3 bytes) -> '__pos (which is 12) > this->size() (which is 11)' = 8+3=11. W="日本語:" (10 bytes) -> 19 > 18. W = 100*'z' + ':' (101 bytes) -> 110 > 109.
Long inputs behave identically (no truncation/limits): W = 500*'A' -> 499-byte result; W = "Mod::" + 300*'B' -> 299-byte result of all 'B' (last colon at index 12, substr(14)).
stdout produced before the throw IS flushed (std::endl flushes): crashing runs still emit the first 4 lines (pluralize, camelize, isPlural, isSingular) before aborting.

The 'no colon anywhere' case is unreachable through this driver because "Module::" is always prepended, so it cannot be observed. If the source literally is `s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2)`, npos + 2 wraps to 1 and the C++ result would be s.substr(1) — which itself throws only for an empty s. A port only needs to be correct for inputs containing ':'.

uncertainties: The behavior when the input contains NO ':' at all is unobservable through this driver ("Module::" is always prepended). If the source is literally `s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2)`, then npos+2 wraps to 1 and C++ would return s.substr(1) (throwing only for empty s). If instead there is a guard (`if (pos == npos) return s;`), the result would be s unchanged. I could not discriminate these. Recommendation for a port: only the has-colon path needs to be byte-exact; for the no-colon path pick a safe fallback (return the input unchanged) and document it, since no test can exercise it via this driver.

Cannot distinguish `rfind(':')` from `find_last_of(":")` / a manual reverse scan for byte 0x3A — they are behaviorally identical for a single-character needle, so this is a distinction without a difference.

Cannot distinguish `substr(pos + 2)` from `substr(pos + 1 + 1)` or from "take the suffix after the last colon then drop its first byte" — identical outputs AND identical crash set for all reachable inputs, except that the two-step form would report a different __pos in the exception text; the observed exception text matches the single-substr form, so the single-substr form is the one to port.
NUL bytes inside the string cannot be tested (execve/argv is NUL-terminated), so behavior for embedded 0x00 is unknown; a byte-faithful port will handle it naturally.

Whether the thrown exception type/message must be reproduced by a port is a policy question. A Rust port would presumably return Err/panic; the exact C++ stderr text and SIGABRT (status 134) are recorded in the goldens if byte-exact process behavior is required.
